definition: Too pleased with yourself in a way that annoys other people.
example: He gave a smug little grin after correcting the tour guide's date.
nuance: Smug stresses visible, irritating self-satisfaction; complacent stresses a lazy sense of security that overlooks danger.
prompt: A student shows off after winning the class spelling bee.
options: With a smug grin, she reminded everyone she had never misspelled a word.
The smug sweater she wore kept her warm on the long walk home.
Smug about her win, she quietly praised the runner-up and gave the credit to luck.
Her smug smile showed how nervous she still felt about the final round.
reasons: Bragging with a self-satisfied grin is the off-putting pride the word describes.
This confuses it with snug; clothing can't be smug, since the word describes attitude.
Modestly crediting others and luck is humility, the reverse of the word.
Nervousness is self-doubt, not pleased self-regard.

practice.prompt: A veteran chess player expects to beat a newcomer easily.
options: Feeling smug, the veteran admitted the newcomer might be the stronger player.
The veteran wiped a smug off the glass face of the chess clock.
Feeling smug, the veteran trembled and asked for extra time on every move.
Feeling smug, the veteran barely glanced at the board between moves.
reasons: Admitting someone else may be better shows humility, not self-satisfaction.
This confuses it with smudge; the word is an adjective for attitude, not a mark.
Trembling and needing more time point to anxiety, which is the opposite of the word.
Showing off your confidence by ignoring your opponent fits the word.
